Thus have I heard: [One time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇ
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna was living in excessive association with the bhikkhunīs.
The Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna lived in such association with the bhikkhunīs as follows:

If any bhikkhu speaks dispraise of those bhikkhunīs in the presence of the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna becomes angry and displeased, and he even initiates a legal dispute over it.
But if any bhikkhu speaks dispraise of the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna in the presence of those bhikkhunīs, those bhikkhunīs become angry and displeased, and they too initiate a legal dispute over it.
In this way, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna dwells closely associated with the bhikkhunīs.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna dwells in excessive association with the bhikkhunīs.
Venerable sir, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna dwells associated with the bhikkhunīs in such a manner.”
“If any bhikkhu speaks dispraise of those bhikkhunīs in the presence of the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna becomes angry and displeased and initiates a legal dispute.
But if any bhikkhu speaks dispraise of the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna in the presence of those bhikkhunīs, those bhikkhunīs become angry and displeased and initiate a legal dispute.
Thus, Bhante, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna dwells in close association with the bhikkhunīs.”
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, address the bhikkhu Moḷiyaphagguna in my name, saying:
‘Friend Phagguna, the Teacher calls for you.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. He then approached the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna and said to him, “Friend Phagguna, the Teacher summons you.
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna replied to that bhikkhu, and he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Is it true, Phagguna, that you dwell excessively in close association with the bhikkhunīs?”

"It seems, Phagguna, that you live in such close association with the bhikkhunīs that if any bhikkhu speaks dispraise of those bhikkhunīs in your presence, you become angry and displeased and even initiate a legal dispute;
yet if any bhikkhu speaks dispraise of you in the presence of those bhikkhunīs, they too become angry and displeased and even initiate a legal dispute."
“Is it true, Phagguna, that you live in close association with the bhikkhunīs?
“Yes, Bhante.
“But, Phagguna, are you not a clansman who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Phagguna, it is not fitting for you—a clansman who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith—to dwell in excessive association with bhikkhunīs.
Therefore, Phagguna, even if someone were to speak dispraise of those bhikkhunīs in your presence, you should abandon any worldly desires and any worldly thoughts regarding them.”
In this regard too, Phagguna, you should train yourself thus:
‘My mind shall not become disturbed, nor shall I utter evil speech; I shall dwell with a heart of loving-kindness, compassionate and seeking their welfare, without harboring ill will.
Thus, Phagguna, should you train yourself.
Therefore, Phagguna, even if someone were to strike those bhikkhunīs in your presence with the hand,
with a clod of earth, with a staff, or with a sword—
you should abandon there, Phagguna, whatever worldly desires and whatever worldly thoughts you may have.
In that regard also, Phagguna, you should train yourself thus:
"My mind shall not become corrupted, nor shall I utter evil speech; rather, I shall dwell sympathetic and compassionate, with a mind of loving-kindness, and not harboring hatred within.
It is in this way, Phagguna, that you should train yourself.
Therefore, Phagguna, even if someone were to speak dispraise of you in your presence, you should abandon there as well those worldly desires and those worldly thoughts.

In that situation too, Phagguna, you should train yourself thus: "My mind shall not become disturbed; I shall not utter evil speech; and I shall dwell sympathetic and compassionate, with a mind of loving-kindness, without internal hatred.
It is in this way, Phagguna, that you should train yourself.
Therefore, Phagguna, even if someone were to strike you with their hand, or strike you with a clod of earth,
or strike you with a staff, or strike you with a sword, even in that situation, Phagguna,
you should abandon those desires based on the household life and those thoughts based on the household life.

"In that regard too, Phagguna, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind shall not become disturbed, nor shall I utter evil speech; rather, I shall dwell compassionate and sympathetic, with a mind of loving-kindness, and not harbor ill will.
In this way, Phagguna, you should train yourself.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, on one occasion my bhikkhus pleased my mind.
Here, bhikkhus, I addressed the bhikkhus thus:
‘Bhikkhus, I eat at a single sitting.’”
“Bhikkhus, when I eat at a single sitting, I experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding.
Come, bhikkhus, you too should eat at a single sitting.
When you eat at a single sitting, bhikkhus, you too will experience freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding.”
“Bhikkhus, no instruction needed to be given by me to those bhikkhus;
rather, bhikkhus, it was only necessary for mindfulness to arise in them.
Just as, bhikkhus, a chariot harnessed with thoroughbred horses might stand on level ground at a crossroads, with the goad lying at hand.”

Just as a skilled horse trainer, a master of taming horses, having mounted that horse, takes the reins in his left hand and the whip in his right hand, can drive it wherever he wishes and bring it back whenever he wishes;
even so, monks, no further instruction needed to be given by me to those bhikkhus.
For them, monks, it was sufficient for me simply to arouse mindfulness.
"Therefore, monks, you too should abandon what is unwholesome and apply yourselves to wholesome states.
In this way, you too will attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
It is just as if, monks, not far from a village or a town, there were a great forest of sal trees."
And it was covered with creepers.
Suppose a certain man were to arise who desired his welfare, his benefit, and his security from bondage;
he would cut down those crooked *sālala* saplings that suck away the vitality and carry them outside, and would thoroughly clear the interior of the forest.
"But those sal-tree trunks that are straight and well-formed, one should properly tend to them.
In this way, monks, this sal forest might at a later time attain growth, increase, and abundance.
Even so, monks, you too should abandon what is unwholesome and apply yourselves to wholesome states."
In this way, you too shall attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Once upon a time, monks, there was a housewife in this very Sāvatthī named Vedehikā.
Regarding that housewife Vedehikā, monks, an excellent reputation had spread abroad:
‘The housewife Vedehikā is gentle; the housewife Vedehikā is free from agitation; the housewife Vedehikā is tranquil.
Now, monks, the housewife Vedehikā had a slave girl named Kālī who was skillful, diligent, and well-organized in her work.
Then, monks, it occurred to the slave girl Kālī:
“Noble lady, such a fine reputation has indeed spread concerning me:
‘Vedehikā, the housewife, is gentle; Vedehikā, the housewife, is free from ill-will; Vedehikā, the housewife, is tranquil.
Now, does my noble lady fail to manifest anger that actually exists within her, or does she not manifest anger that does not exist?”
"Or is it that these tasks of mine are so well-arranged that my mistress does not manifest anger within herself when it actually exists, nor when it does not exist?
What if I were to test my mistress?
Then, monks, the slave girl Kālī rose up during the day.
Then, monks, the housewife Vedehikā said this to her maidservant Kālī:
“Hey, Kālī! “What is it, mistress? she asked.
"What, girl, have you been doing standing up all day?
"Nothing at all, mistress. "Nothing at all?
You wicked slave, you have been standing up all day! she said, becoming angry and displeased, and she knit her brows in a frown.
Then, monks, it occurred to the maidservant Kāḷī:
“It is only when anger is actually present within my mistress that she does not manifest it, not when it is absent.
These very tasks of mine are so well-arranged that my mistress does not manifest anger within herself even when it is actually present, let alone when it is absent.”
"What if I were to test my mistress even more thoroughly?
Then, monks, the slave girl Kālī rose very early in the morning.
Then, monks, the housewife Vedehikā said this to the slave girl Kālī:
“‘It is Kālī.
‘What is it, noble lady?
‘Why, girl, did you rise so much earlier?’”
“‘Nothing at all, my lady,’ she replied.
‘Oh, nothing at all! You wicked slave, you have risen even earlier than usual! Thus, angry and displeased, she uttered words of displeasure.
Then, monks, it occurred to the slave girl Kāḷī:”
‘The mistress does not manifest anger within herself when it actually exists, nor when it does not exist.
These tasks of mine are well-arranged, such that the mistress does not manifest anger within herself when it actually exists, nor when it does not exist.
What if I were to test her even further?’
Then, monks, the slave girl Kālī rose quite early in the morning.
Then, monks, the housewife Vedehikā said this to the slave girl Kālī:
“Hey, girl Kālī!”
“What is it, noble lady?
“What is it, girl? Why did you get up during the day?
“It was nothing at all, noble lady.”
“‘Oh, you wicked slave! You have not risen at all today! Thus, angry and displeased, she took a door-bolt and struck her on the head, splitting it open.
Then, monks, with her head split and blood flowing, the slave Kālī complained to her neighbors:
‘See, ladies, the deed of this gentle woman!’”
"Look, ladies, at the work of one who lives in security! Look, ladies, at the work of one who lives in peace!
How could she, being a single slave-woman, rise so early in the day? Being angry and displeased, she has taken a door-pin and struck her on the head, even piercing her skull!
Then, monks, at a later time, a wicked report concerning the housewife Vedehikā spread abroad:
‘Vedehikā the housewife is fierce; Vedehikā the housewife is unyielding; Vedehikā the housewife is unpacified.

In the same way, monks, here a certain monk is as gentle as a gentle person, as yielding as a yielding person, and as pacified as a pacified person—only so long as disagreeable paths of speech do not touch him.
But when, monks, disagreeable paths of speech do touch a monk, then that monk should be known as ‘gentle,’ he should be known as ‘yielding,’ and he should be known as ‘pacified.’
“Monks, I do not call that monk ‘easily spoken to’ who is easily spoken to and becomes compliant for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Why is that?
Because, monks, when that monk does not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he is no longer easily spoken to, nor does he become compliant.”
But as for that monk, bhikkhus, who honors the Dhamma alone, respects the Dhamma, reveres the Dhamma,
worships the Dhamma, and pays homage to the Dhamma, and who is easy to speak to and adopts a disposition of being easy to speak to—
I call him "one who is easy to speak to."

"Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: 'Honoring the Dhamma alone, respecting the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, worshipping the Dhamma, and venerating the Dhamma, we shall be easy to speak to; we shall attain the state of being easy to speak to.
For these, bhikkhus, are the five ways of speaking by which others might address you when they speak."
Whether at the right time or at the wrong time;
whether in truth or in falsehood;
whether gently or harshly.
Whether it be connected with benefit or not connected with benefit;
whether they speak with a mind of loving-kindness or with internal hatred;
whether, monks, others might speak at the proper time or at the improper time;
Monks, others may speak to you with what is true or with what is untrue;
they may speak to you gently or harshly;
they may speak to you with what is beneficial or with what is not beneficial.
“Monks, even if others should speak to you with minds of loving-kindness or with minds of ill will, in that situation too, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

‘Our minds shall not become disturbed, nor shall we utter evil speech; rather, we shall dwell with thoughts of loving-kindness, compassionate and seeking their welfare, and not with minds of ill will.’”
‘Having pervaded that person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, we shall dwell;
and having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—
we shall dwell.’”
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Suppose, monks, a man were to come along carrying a spade and a basket.
He would say this:"
‘I shall turn this great earth into non-earth.
He would dig here and there, scatter it here and there, spit upon it here and there, and drench it here and there, saying:
‘Become non-earth! Become non-earth!’
“What do you think, bhikkhus,
would that man turn this great earth into non-earth?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And why is that? “Because, Bhante, this great earth is deep and immeasurable;
it is not easy to turn it into non-earth.”
“And furthermore, that man would only partake of exhaustion and distress.
“In the same way, monks, there are these five modes of speech by which others might speak to you—
whether at the proper time or at the improper time;”
Whether it be true or false;
whether gentle or harsh;
whether beneficial or unbeneficial.
Whether they have a mind of loving-kindness or harbor ill will;
whether others speak at the proper time or at the improper time, monks;
whether others speak what is true or what is untrue, monks.
Monks, others might speak to you either gently or harshly;
they might speak to you with what is beneficial or with what is unbeneficial;
others might speak to you with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hatred.
In that regard too, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"Our minds shall not become disturbed, nor shall we utter evil speech; we shall dwell with kindness and compassion, with hearts of loving-kindness and free from ill will.
Having pervaded that person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, we shall dwell pervading the entire world with that as our object."
‘We shall dwell pervading the world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
Just as if, monks, a man were to come along carrying lac, or turmeric, or indigo, or madder.
Suppose someone were to say this:
‘I shall paint a form in this space; I shall bring about the manifestation of a form.
What do you think, monks?
“Would that man, then, be able to paint a form in this space, or bring about the manifestation of a form?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“And for what reason?”
“Venerable sir, this space is formless and non-manifest.
It is not easy to paint a form there, nor to make a form appear;
at best, that person would only experience exhaustion and frustration.”
“In the same way, bhikkhus, there are these five ways of speaking by which others might speak to you, whether at the right time or the wrong time...
[and so on]... ‘Having pervaded the entire world with a mind endowed with that object—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—we shall dwell.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves.”
“Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to come along carrying a burning grass torch and say:
‘With this burning grass torch, I shall heat and thoroughly scorch the river Ganges.’”
“What do you think, monks,
would that man be able to heat or thoroughly scorch the river Ganges with a burning grass torch?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, venerable sir, the river Ganges is deep and immeasurable.
It is not easy to heat it thoroughly or to make it boil with a burning grass torch.”
“And furthermore, that man would only partake of fatigue and vexation.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, there are these five ways of speaking by which others might speak to you, whether at the right time or the wrong time... [as before] ...
‘Having pervaded the entire world with a mind like the Ganges—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—we shall dwell therein.’”
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves. Just as if, monks,
there were a cat-skin bag that had been well-beaten, thoroughly beaten, and completely rubbed down— soft, fluffy, with its rustling sound silenced and its crackling sound silenced—
and then a man were to come along carrying a piece of wood or a pebble."
Suppose someone were to say:

‘I shall make this cat’s skin—thoroughly rubbed, well-rubbed, and perfectly rubbed, soft and woolly, with its bristling hairs cut away and its downy hair cut away—resound with a rustling sound by means of a stick or a potsherd;
I shall make it produce a booming sound. What do you think, monks?
“Would that man, by rubbing and kneading that cat-skin bag— well-massaged, well-kneaded, well-pressed, soft, fluffy,
with its rustling sound cut out and its crackling noise silenced— be able to make it rustle or crackle with a stick or a pebble?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, venerable sir, that cat’s skin has been well-beaten, thoroughly beaten, and well-massaged; it is soft and downy, with its hair and fur removed.
It is not easy to make it produce a rustling sound or a crackling sound by means of a stick or a pebble.”
"And furthermore, that man would only partake in exhaustion and frustration.
"In the same way, monks, there are these five ways of speaking by which others might speak to you,
whether at the proper time or at an improper time:"
Whether it be true or false;
whether gentle or harsh;
whether beneficial or unbeneficial.
Whether with a mind of loving-kindness or with internal hatred;
whether others might speak at the proper time or at the improper time, monks;
whether others might speak what is true or what is untrue, monks.
Monks, others might speak to you either gently or harshly;
they might speak to you with what is beneficial or with what is unbeneficial;
others might speak to you with a mind of loving-kindness or with internal hatred.
In that regard too, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"Our minds shall not become disturbed, nor shall we utter evil speech; we shall dwell with kindness and compassion, with hearts of loving-kindness and free from ill will.
And we shall dwell pervading that person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the entire world surrounding them as its object."
‘We shall dwell pervading the world with a mind [vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will],
like a cat’s-paw bag,’ thus, monks, should you train yourselves.

“Monks, even if bandits with saws having double handles were to hack away at your limbs one by one, whoever should allow their mind to become corrupted therein would not be following my teaching because of that.
In such a situation, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘Our minds shall not be disturbed, we shall not utter evil speech, and we shall dwell compassionate and sympathetic, with hearts of loving-kindness and free from ill will.’”
‘Having pervaded that person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, we shall dwell;
and having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—
we shall dwell.’”
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
And you, monks, should frequently bring to mind this instruction on the simile of the saw.
Do you see, monks, any course of speech—whether subtle or gross—that you would not endure?"
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, constantly attend to this simile of the saw.
That will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The monks were delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The First Discourse, the Simile of the Saw, is finished.
